title: Faith as a dark light (Ascent 2)
hookLine: faith guides like a light we can't look at directly

lines: A LIGHT THAT FEELS LIKE DARK.
cards: Driving a country road at night, you never see your own headlights. You see by them: the white line, the edge of the ditch, a deer by the fence, a few yards of road at a time. Beyond that, black.
You couldn't describe the light itself, and yet everything you see out there comes through it. John of the Cross says faith works something like that. It's a light.
But from the inside, it feels like darkness.

teach.h: FAITH IS DARK TO THE MIND.
teach.b: First, a dark night. In the second book of the Ascent, John calls faith itself a dark night for the soul. Faith asks us to trust what we can't see, touch or prove, on the word of God.
That's dark to the mind, which wants to see for itself. But, he adds, the darker it is for the mind, the more light it gives the soul. Second, the cloud.
John points to the Exodus story. As Israel escapes Egypt, a pillar of cloud stands between them and the army chasing them.

teach.h: A DARK CLOUD THAT LIGHTS THE NIGHT.
teach.b: The Douay-Rheims says: "it was a dark cloud, and enlightening the night." Dark on one side, light on the other. The same cloud.
That's faith, John says: darkness to our understanding, light for our way. Third, the walk. Saint Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we walk by faith, and not by sight."
Walking isn't understanding. You can walk a path whose end you can't see, one step, in trust.
Fourth, why not visions? John warns against chasing visions, voices and special signs. They can mislead, he says, and even true ones can become something to cling to.

teach.h: FOR WE WALK BY FAITH, AND NOT BY SIGHT.
teach.b: Faith is the surer guide, precisely because it's plain, humble and dark. Now look back at the week. One dark night, and a house at rest.
Sweetness: dry is not gone. Three signs: the longing stays. Isaiah: bigger than your idea.
Nada: nothing, then everything. A bird on a thread. And today, a light we can't look at but see by.

how: Catholics describe faith as trust in what God has revealed rather than in what they can see or prove, and spiritual directors in the Carmelite tradition steer people away from seeking visions toward plain faith.

o: John's picture of faith: dark to the mind, light for the way
a storm sent as a sign that God is displeased with you
a heavy sadness that hides God from the soul for a while

games.q: what's inside the dark light — tap the pairs.
p: you can't look at it, you see by it

s: John says faith is a bright, clear light to the mind
he calls faith a dark night for the mind, and yet a light for the soul.
John uses the Exodus cloud as a picture of faith
a dark cloud that also lit up the night.
John says visions are the surest guide
he says faith is surer; visions can mislead, and even true ones can be clung to.

games.q: you're praying about a hard decision, and you wish God would just send a clear sign. what does John advise?
o: ask for a vision and wait for it.
walk by plain faith, one step at a time.
games.why: John says not to chase signs. faith is dark, but it's the surer light for the way.

practice: Think of something unresolved in your life, where you can't see the end: a diagnosis, a job, a child's choices, a question about God. Don't try to solve it; picture it as a path in the dark, and yourself taking just one step.
If you pray, hand the unseen part to God and ask only for the next step; if you don't, name the one step you can see.

wordCard.voice: Dark cloud. The image from Exodus John uses for faith in the Ascent: dark to our understanding on one side, yet lighting our way on the other. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: walk by faith. One step at a time is still walking. A week of night, done.
